name: Hair-grooming syncope awareness

card.summary: Knowing that combing, brushing or cutting hair can trigger fainting in some people, so grooming routines stay safe and uninterrupted.
card.note: Described in paediatric case series as a benign reflex faint; injury from falling is the main concern.

quick.overview:
Hair-grooming syncope is a rare form of reflex (neurocardiogenic) fainting triggered by hair care such as brushing, combing, braiding or cutting. Awareness of it helps people who have fainted while grooming recognise the pattern and keep their hair routines going safely.

The appearance connection is practical: grooming is a daily part of looking presentable, and understanding a trigger lets people continue styling safely rather than stopping or being surprised by a faint.
quick.how: There is no product or technique; awareness means recognising that grooming can be a trigger and discussing episodes with a clinician. Reported cases were evaluated with cardiology exams and tilt-table testing.
quick.risks: Reported cases were benign, with normal heart tests, but fainting can cause injury by falling. Anyone who loses consciousness should be assessed by a doctor to rule out other causes.

lead: Hair-grooming syncope is a rare, benign form of reflex fainting in which hair care such as combing, brushing or cutting triggers a brief loss of consciousness. It has been described mainly in children and adolescents in cardiology and paediatric literature [1][2][3].

A 1996 Spanish series described four girls averaging 9.5 years old who fainted briefly in relation to hair care; tilt testing was positive in three, and the authors considered it a benign variant of neurocardiogenic syncope [1]. A later 2009 review of 1,525 children with syncope found 111 with a hair-grooming trigger; 78% were girls, boys fainted more during hair cutting and girls during combing and brushing, and heart tests were unremarkable [3].

chain: Recognise that grooming can trigger a reflex faint
Understand it as a benign vasovagal pattern
angle.text: For people whose grooming has triggered faints, knowing the cause supports safe styling and haircuts. It does not change how hair looks.

infobox: Mostly children; 78% girls in one series [3]

paras: Situational syncope occurs when a specific activity triggers a vagal reflex that lowers heart rate or blood pressure and briefly reduces blood flow to the brain [4]. Hair grooming is one recognised trigger, alongside others in the situational group [1][3].
A related report documented asystole, a brief heart pause, caused by head scratching [5].
Medical sources on situational syncope say the main danger is injury from falling; avoiding known triggers, lying down when warning signs appear and moving to a safe spot are the usual guidance [4].

A 1993 report described hair-grooming syncope in the context of seizures [2]. The 1996 case series of four girls [1] and a 2009 series of 111 children [3] are the main published descriptions; both found it benign, and the larger series found normal ECGs and echocardiograms [3].

timeline.event: Spanish case series of four girls [1]
